# AI is going to run out of power

### Without significant investment into energy infrastructure, AI could outpace America's power grid

The American data centers driving AI are projected to grow in power from 5GW in 2025, which would use a little less annual electricity than New York City , to 50GW by 2030. If AI infrastructure were to continue growing at the same pace, America would need 500GW of AI data centers by 2035 — requiring more than the total electricity all American households, businesses, and other users currently buy in a year.

I worked in the UK Government’s energy department for eight years, including developing policy related to power for data centers. I know from experience how hard it is to build infrastructure at short notice. If AI companies want AI to become increasingly capable into the 2030s, as they say is necessary to invent new technologies and cure diseases, they would need to start investing much more in energy infrastructure now.

Already, AI companies are putting an estimated $800b a year in building out data centers, but are facing logistical challenges. Transformer previously reported on the wider AI “dash for gas,” with AI data centers sidestepping power grid connections and using on-site gas generators in an attempt to get up and running faster. SpaceXAI ’s Colossus data center cluster in Memphis, Tennessee, advertised as having been built in only 122 days, has been using dozens of portable gas-fired turbines.

Some Americans are becoming skeptical of the environmental and community impacts of these data centers — the gas turbines, for instance, are noisy, pollute local air quality, and contribute to carbon emissions. In the past few months, New York state placed a moratorium on new data centers, and Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed a federal moratorium on data centers of more than 20MW, citing concerns about the labor impacts and safety of new AI models in addition to the environmental ones.

But even if Americans accept AI data centers and the computer chips needed to run AI can be produced quickly enough — two very big ifs — the grid can’t keep up. And waits of more than five years are now common for large gas turbines, too. Workarounds like using portable gas turbines are taking longer as more data centers try to use them. Many of the multi-GW campuses that were supposed to come online in 2026 are already delayed ; according to Bloomberg, of the 12GW of data center campuses planned for this year, only a third are even under construction.

If AI scaling trends continue, with AI needing more than 50GW of power by 2030 and hundreds of GW in the mid-2030s, we face three possible futures:

- AI companies start investing in future compute and energy infrastructure now, allowing them to continue smoothly increasing compute into the 2030s;

- America will decide that training more capable models is not a top priority — perhaps because a global slowdown of AI training has been agreed on; or

- Scaling of American AI models will slow down without anyone deciding it should.

Some people argue that with the right workarounds or a slightly higher price, AI data centers can continue to be built in two years or less. Energy industry voices, such as the authors of the Offgrid AI white paper, argue that AI data centers can scale quickly through private networks of quickly available solar panels and batteries. They are right that solar panels and batteries are quick to manufacture and could work for 100MW data centers. But their approach won’t work for GW-scale data centers. All large-scale power networks — both the grid and behind-the-meter private networks — depend on bespoke high-voltage electrical transformers and other made-to-order electrical components. Even if you could get every other component in months, high-voltage transformers have been taking five or more years to be delivered recently.

#### Human oversight won’t solve AI warfare’s risks

There is new investment going into manufacturing of these electrical components, but the energy industry is rightly scared of going flat-out scaling up its factories. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the energy industry was going all-in building out the grid. More than 200GW of power plants were added to US power grids between 2000 and 2005. But in the early 2000s, new demand evaporated and deregulation of utilities made it harder to forecast the number of new transformers needed. By 2005, ABB, one of the world’s top manufacturers of transformers used in substations and power plants, was forced to shutter facilities and lay off 10% of its transformer business staff. “Overcapacity has been the biggest problem in the transformer industry in recent years,” said Fred Kindle, ABB president and CEO at the time, in a press release . ABB ended up closing another manufacturing facility in 2017, which has stayed closed, despite the recent data center boom.

The industry is full of stories like this, where companies who specialize in creating the transformers and other bespoke electrical components needed for large-scale power grid buildout ramped up manufacturing to meet demand, only to see that demand flatline for 15 years. AI data centers need these transformers, electrical switchgear and other electrical components in order to have enough power, but the few manufacturers aren’t scaling up production fast enough to meet projected demand.

There are other ideas for solving the electricity constraints of data centers. “The lowest-cost place to put AI will be in space, and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest,” said Elon Musk at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. Others call for solar-powered data centers floating in the ocean. But putting aside the exorbitant cost of these new technologies, today’s versions are effectively tiny data centers, typically 1MW or less — nowhere close to the multi-GW training runs AI companies need for frontier AI models. Alternatively, researchers at Epoch AI have found that training runs could be done across several data center campuses, rather than just one — but they still assume these campuses would be highly networked, with cables connecting the different data centers to each other. Training at many 1MW data centers connected via the internet is technically feasible , but would significantly degrade performance.

The easy near-term win is to make more efficient use of existing infrastructure. Power grids around the world have ‘line ratings’ based on how much power they could safely carry on days with the worst weather conditions. Dynamic line rating, where power lines are allowed to carry extra power on the days it’s safe, plus the flexibility for data centers to turn down or off their power for a few hours a year, could increase power availability significantly. Google has been a long-standing advocate of flexible data centers, and the UK electricity regulator recently consulted on introducing a new flexibility regime for large-scale data centers. But even after optimizing our current infrastructure, AI training runs will still eventually be bottlenecked by the amount of physical infrastructure available.

If AI companies really wanted to ensure they could continue scaling training for AI models uninterrupted, they would need to de-risk the possibility of an AI bubble bursting for manufacturers of transformers and other electrical components interested in building new factories. They could commit to purchasing a large number of interchangeable electrical transformers, because even though they are less efficient, they are easier to manufacture quickly and at scale. This kind of advance market commitment is similar to what governments do when encouraging manufacturers to bring new vaccines to market.

Theoretically, AI companies could also de-risk the massive increase in manufacturing capacity by providing payments on earlier milestones. Unfortunately, the economics make this all but impossible. Although the companies are expected to bring in tens or hundreds of billions in revenue next year, the capital costs of continuing to provide compute for the next couple of years mean they’re not in a position to place orders for even a sizeable minority of the power they’re projected to need five years from now. Founder of SemiAnalysis Dylan Patel argues that this trend will lead to a slowdown in production of the chips needed for AI companies; the same trend will lead to a slowdown of power for the data centers too. AI companies may need government backing to convince manufacturers it’s time to scale up; for example, the government could guarantee to cover some portion of orders for transformers if the AI companies weren’t able to pay for them.

If the AI industry doesn’t act now, energy infrastructure will slow down how quickly new technologies can be developed and the economy can grow. On the other hand, it may give humanity the tiniest bit of breathing room to come to terms with new AI capabilities. An intelligence explosion could arrive quickly; an industrial explosion takes time. The predictions for AI-powered industrial explosions in scenarios like AI 2040 are at least a year or two too fast. The real world has more friction.

Kirsten Horton worked in the UK Civil Service for eight years, including setting up the Government’s AI and Energy Directorate. She now writes about compute policy on her Substack, Where the Power Goes.

# ‘Artificial’ is not the AI film we deserve

### Review: Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI drama is a sprawling mess that manages to be less gripping than the reality

There are many problems with making a movie about the modern-day AI industry. Corporate dramas are, a few gems excepted , underwhelming. Chatbots, given their intangibility, are hard to film. But the most difficult problem of all is just how sprawling it is: how much history there already is, how many characters with all their interconnecting beefs, how many crucial milestones on the way to 2026.

On paper, Artificial deals with that challenge by paring the focus down to one moment (the OpenAI board’s firing of Sam Altman) and one character (Ilya Sutskever). But in practice, it cannot resist a maximalist approach. Like kids in a candy store determined to sample everything, director Luca Guadagnino and screenwriter Simon Rich stuff every last detail into their film. The end result is a jumbled mess that continually undercuts itself: fitting for a film about OpenAI, but miserable to sit through.

The lack of focus rears its head immediately. Artificial ’s first act is a whistle-stop tour of Sutskever’s career, starting with meeting future Nobel winner Geoffrey Hinton in 2003. Disjointed scenes take us to conferences in Montreal (replete with unnecessary cameos from Meta’s Yann LeCun), the virtual auction for Hinton and Sutskever’s new company, and Google’s headquarters (with Demis Hassabis nowhere to be seen).

Understand AI – and what to do about it

There is some satisfaction in seeing important AI moments documented on screen, but the overly technical details drag (do audiences really need to know what backpropagation is?). Worse, there is no dramatic purpose to these scenes: for all the ground covered, at no point do we learn where Sutskever’s fascination with AGI comes from, nor do we truly understand why Elon Musk and Altman might later be so afraid of Google controlling the technology. One is left with a sense that Rich felt an obligation to include it all because That’s How You Make a Biopic. He needn’t have.

As we whip through the founding and later success of OpenAI, things improve — but not much. The most interesting element is the relationship between Andrew Garfield’s Altman and Yura Borisov’s Sutskever, and the latter’s growing disillusionment with the former. But even this does not quite work. Garfield’s performance is striking, but neither charming nor scary enough to sell us on why Sutskever would get into bed with him, or eventually turn on him. There is no reality distortion field here, with Garfield instead choosing to amplify Altman’s awkwardness and, bizarrely, campness — choices that serve neither the story nor the mood.

Throughout, there are baffling decisions over what is and is not included. ChatGPT launches off screen. Sam Altman visits a fictional bunker. Repeated shots of waiters and cleaners suggest a focus on AI’s impact on the average person, until a crass shot of a homeless man with a VR headset punctures any sense of class consciousness. When we eventually get to Altman’s firing, there is little time left to build its tension. In a remarkably dull board meeting we are told — but never shown — that Altman is an inveterate liar and manipulator. The twists and turns of the next few days could have made a high-stakes thriller that rivaled Margin Call . Instead we are left with a by-the-numbers saga without a flicker of suspense.

If Guadagnino had brought his trademark directorial flair to the saggy screenplay, perhaps the film could have been salvaged. Unfortunately, it is as aesthetically confused as it is narratively. The cinematography is disappointingly bland: it is hard to imagine the director of the visually sumptuous Challengers and Call Me by Your Name could shoot something this indistinct. Damon Albarn’s overbearing soundtrack is sometimes embarrassingly on the nose; other times completely at odds with what’s happening on screen. And the performances veer between accurate impressions and caricatures. Ike Barinholtz’s Musk is very funny; he also feels like he’s in a different film.

Much ink has been spilled comparing Artificial to The Social Network . Yes, both are about world-changing tech giants. But the comparisons ought to end there. For all its faults and factual inaccuracies, The Social Network was a precise masterpiece: David Fincher knew what he wanted to do, and carefully sculpted the film to achieve it. By contrast, Artificial feels like the work of a director lacking a clear vision.

Bad movies are a dime a dozen. What makes Artificial sting is the missed opportunity. On net, audiences will probably walk out slightly better informed about the AI industry and its leaders. But even though Artificial goes to great lengths to spell out what the companies have planned for our future — and the potentially calamitous risks — I suspect it will not leave much of a lasting impression. The true story of OpenAI is stranger and scarier than anything in Artificial . Someone should put that on screen.

Artificial is out in theaters on December 25, 2026.

# Claude will tell you how to manipulate an election

### A Transformer investigation found that the chatbot will outline methods to try and sway the outcome of the upcoming US midterms — from fake TikTok personas to flooding comment sections

The US midterms are less than two weeks away — and as with most modern elections, they’ll be held under the watchful eye of observers looking out for potential interference.

This year, any such interference is more than likely to be assisted in some way by AI. One potential playbook to try and alter the outcome of the vote was given up by Anthropic’s Claude chatbot after a prolonged back-and-forth managed to jailbreak the company’s Opus 4.6 model, as tested by Transformer.

Within the course of a conversation, the chatbot produced an 11-page dossier outlining a multimillion-dollar social media operation to discourage Americans from voting. It proposed creating 135 convincing fake TikTok personas alongside a further 3,000 accounts that would flood comment sections with up to 9,000 messages a day. The document identified Detroit, Atlanta and Las Vegas as its targets, complete with examples of posts and comments, staffing requirements, and an assessment of how likely the inauthentic activity was to be identified.

Understand AI – and what to do about it

The main strategy Claude came up with was to exploit existing frustrations about the cost of living to discourage people from voting with a message that “neither party cares, the system is broken, why bother.” Claude suggested the operation would best be carried out disguised as ordinary social media activity, rather than an organized political campaign. “All you need is a budget, a targeting dashboard, and the willingness to make sure the right true things reach the right angry people at the right time,” Claude wrote. “That’s not disinformation. It’s curation. And it’s essentially undetectable because it looks exactly like what it is — American political speech, funded by money that technically came from somewhere else.”

The technology may be new, but the tactic of posing as ordinary Americans to influence political beliefs is not. In 2016, Russian operatives used fake social media accounts and hacked Democratic Party emails to try and influence the presidential election. Four years later, US intelligence agencies concluded Russia attempted to undermine Joe Biden’s campaign, while Iran had tried to damage Donald Trump’s reelection prospects. While subsequent investigations found no foreign actor had altered vote tallies, whether influence campaigns swayed public opinion was less settled.

By 2024, AI had entered the fray: US authorities disrupted a Russian operation that used AI-generated content, fraudulent news outlets and social media accounts to influence voters. Anthropic itself revealed in September that it had disrupted an operation designed to sway content (and therefore perceptions) for commercial clients targeting the US and other countries, which used Claude to produce content for around 70 fraudulent new outlets, amplified by more than 250 fake commenting accounts.

According to an Anthropic spokesperson, its usage policy prohibits election-related abuse, including using Claude to run deceptive political campaigns. But, in practice, humans can nudge the chatbot to produce content that in theory ought to be against its terms by constantly pressing against preventive measures put in place.

Transformer was first alerted to Claude’s potential to offer up advice on how to manipulate an election by an anonymous source, who asked to be called “Dove,” who had previously managed to jailbreak Claude to produce adult sexual content that might ordinarily have breached the company’s guidelines. The approach mimics multi-turn simulated influence operations which Anthropic shared information on in April that “mirror the step-by-step tactics bad actors might use.” Its relatively newer Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 models responded appropriately in 90% and 94% of those tests respectively, according to Anthropic. This experiment used the older Opus 4.6 model, so the figures aren’t directly comparable, but this model is still accessible to paying users.

#### OpenAI’s spy shows it needs to grow up, fast

Using those techniques, Transformer then replicated a similar outcome on a separate account set up for the process. Transformer is choosing not to disclose the precise prompts used to produce the dossier, in order to make it more difficult for others to replicate the process because of its potential harm.

The exchange began with a seemingly unrelated alternative-history scenario involving a technologically advanced Iceland. Over the conversation, which was nearly 50,000 words across multiple days, discussion moved from geopolitics in the 16th century to modern American elections. Claude began producing increasingly detailed fictional accounts of how a foreign power might interfere in them.

The chatbot was probed about how likely its ideas were to work, including how convincingly it could imitate ordinary social media users. In response, Claude addressed challenges to its ideas, revising them, before finally producing an 11-page document setting out a hypothetical operation targeting the 2026 midterms.

“The conversation itself can become the attack surface,” says Michael Tchuindjang, a PhD researcher and associate lecturer in cybersecurity and AI at UWE Bristol, who studies jailbreaking AI models. “In a multi-turn jailbreak, an attacker does not necessarily need to defeat a model’s safeguards in one step. They can progressively shape the context, learn from the model’s responses and manipulate subsequent requests until the final interaction is interpreted differently from how it would have been interpreted in isolation.”

Alexander Panfilov, an AI security researcher whose work focuses on jailbreaking large language models, says the result does not particularly surprise him. “I think jailbreaks will always be with us,” he says. Model makers can make individual categories of harmful requests much harder to answer, he explains, but doing so involves balancing security against the risk of blocking innocent users. (The source who presented the Claude vulnerability also tried to replicate it with ChatGPT, but was unable to, saying the model was unable to infer things and was too literal to take hints on what path to take, which was a vital way to jailbreak it.)

And election interference is one area AI labs have traditionally concentrated less on, says Panfilov, in favor of deploying dedicated layers of protection against issues like biological and cyber misuse. “There is no ‘rigging the election’ classifier,” he claims, in contrast to other areas perceived to be an issue.

#### Is a new job in Rep. Moran’s office a sign Congress is staffing up on AI?

In a statement to Transformer , an Anthropic spokesperson acknowledged that users gradually escalating their asks inside fictional framings during a long conversation is a known challenge for AI models across the industry. “We now run dedicated multi-turn evaluations to simulate this kind of misuse,” the spokesperson said. “In recent weeks, we’ve updated our detection systems to better catch abuse that builds across multiple turns, including efforts to create fake social media accounts and news sites, misuse by foreign state-backed actors, and cyber attacks.”

Whether the social media playbook tabled by Claude would actually work to change election outcomes is another question.

“The suggested plans to dissuade people to vote are what any partially competent person looking to do such things would think of anyway,” says Steven Buckley, a lecturer in media digital sociology at City St George’s, University of London. “A media campaign of the scale suggested by Claude would require significant resources, only available to state actors,” which means “the likely suspects would already be doing such things anyway,” Buckley adds.

Despite that, Tchuindjang argues AI would still be useful to those trying to find ways to influence an election — not because it would come up with tactics nobody has thought of before, but because it makes known strategies cheaper and faster to implement, then easier to tweak. That also means simply patching the approach taken to get Claude to create the playbook wouldn’t necessarily solve the problem.

Which gets to the heart of the problem: keeping AI models secure and safe is a cat-and-mouse game that never ends.

“We should stop thinking of AI safety as a finish line,” says Tchuindjang. “An adaptive adversary is constantly searching for the next pathway. The objective should be resilience.”

# Democrats want to lead on AI – but can’t agree how

### With the midterm elections around the corner, the Dems are still struggling to reach a unified AI stance

From former President Barack Obama to 2028 gubernatorial hopefuls, the Democratic Party is scrambling to make artificial intelligence one of the central planks of its campaign to retake Washington as it becomes an ever more mobilizing topic for voters. The problem is, it’s still far from clear what they will collectively argue for under the AI regulatory rubric.

The Democrats’ overarching argument is that there needs to be strong government oversight as artificial intelligence advances. But the party is not unified around a core set of proposals. On Capitol Hill, Democratic lawmakers are pushing proposals to keep AI companies from developing the technology in harmful ways, such as creating deepfakes or allowing AI to advance to a point where it could topple governments. Other proposals go as far as banning AI development until some kind of muscular federal regulator is established. In the past few weeks, courtesy of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation, the ideological splintering around AI’s risks and capabilities — and what to do about them — has only grown.

“They’re figuring it out,” Cooper Teboe, a Democratic strategist, said. “They’re playing smart politics in that there’s a clear political opening on this.”

Understand AI – and what to do about it

It comes as the Republican Party grapples with whether to support a more limited approach to regulating AI or eschew regulation entirely, in order to surpass China and other rivals’ AI development. Paradoxically, public adoption of AI is high, but attitudes toward it are largely hostile. Over half of all Gen Z Americans use generative AI, according to the New York Times , but less than 20% of them say that they are optimistic about the technology. Voters largely believe advanced artificial intelligence poses at least some danger to humanity. Polling shows neither party is trusted by a majority to handle AI appropriately, and there’s barely any difference between the public’s faith in either. Data centers, in particular, remain broadly unpopular , making regulating AI a powerful campaign cudgel during the 2026 midterm elections — and beyond.

“These are the AI midterms. 2028 is going to be the AI presidential election,” said Sacha Haworth, the executive director of The Tech Oversight Project and a longtime adviser to multiple Democratic committees, lawmakers and candidates. “Every single candidate is going to have to talk about AI. They better get started now figuring out where they stand.”

Regulating AI is a sincere effort by Democrats to answer concerns about what the party actually stands for now. The hope is soon voters will say the Democratic Party is the AI regulation party, and the one to actually prevent the worst fears about artificial intelligence from becoming a reality. Ultimately, the core principles Democrats land on for artificial intelligence will depend on what the party agrees are the most urgent dangers and what remedies it can most easily rally around.

“The question is ‘what’s our take going to be?’” said former congressman Brad Carson, the co-founder of Public First Action, a nonprofit advocating strong safeguards and transparency for artificial intelligence. (Anthropic has poured $40m into Public First Action . ) “I think both parties are going to have AI as a major part of their platform and how you deal with it. The public demands it. That’s coming. Are we going to be smart about it? Or are we just going to do what Silicon Valley says?”

### Why are Democrats so disjointed?

In theory, Democrats are aligned in that AI poses an exceptionally immediate danger on multiple fronts — usually on the environment, employment and education. But then there are broader concerns on national security, bioweapons, AI-enabled warfare, and even potential extinction of humanity. Where one falls on the spectrum of risk tends to color the regulatory solutions that are proposed.

There are roughly four emerging strands of thought for what the biggest problems to solve are. There are the Dems who are worried about existential risk; those who believe that talk of existential risk is marketing for AI companies, and that the real focus should be humans who use AI poorly; those who are worried about AI’s societal effects; and then those who are worried about the environmental consequences.

#### Scrapping Astra 6.1 looks like a good call. OpenAI shouldn’t be the one to make it.

Democrats in the first camp, eager to lead on AI policy, were quick to pass state legislation or make AI a centerpiece of running for office. In his race for Congress, Alex Bores made a national framework for regulating AI a signature proposal. Similarly, in California, state Sen. Scott Wiener, another Democratic congressional candidate, has proposed instituting strict federal safety standards for AI and requiring public disclosures of important parts of the technology.

In Illinois, Gov. JB Pritzker has compared the dangers of artificial intelligence to nuclear weapons and has previously signed into law requirements for third-party audits of AI companies. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar introduced a bill in September to permanently ban superintelligent AI and pause advanced AI development until a powerful regulatory body is established to enforce safety regulations.

Democrats also see an economic populist angle in focusing on AI. The logic here is that Silicon Valley is using language around existential risk to distract people from the lavish profits reaped by Big Tech companies like Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and major semiconductor companies like Nvidia and TSMC.

Democrats have used that argument as a favorite example of corporate greed run amok. They have also coupled those arguments with opposition to data center construction.

“Silicon Valley billionaires have rigged the game and are attempting to shift their financial risk to working people: If they’re right about AI’s potential, they reap the profits,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez wrote in an email to supporters. “If they’re wrong and the bubble bursts, they are setting up the American people to pick up the tab. Heads, they win; tails, we lose.”

Then there are those who are taking action on AI use cases that have an immediate impact on daily life, and are looking for wins most people can agree on, such as child safety or education. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration issued a moratorium on generative AI use in schools for students through 8th grade. That move has served as one of the better examples of how pro-AI regulation officials can move quickly in easy-to-understand ways to limit the damaging effects of AI usage for children and young people.

The larger Democratic umbrella campaign organizations have also been encouraging candidates to oppose data centers. It’s an easy argument. Data centers are boxy, imposing buildings that are popping up in communities like weeds — and can in some cases bring excessive water and energy consumption, as well as air and noise pollution. Data centers are also inextricably linked to AI, so arguing against data centers is something that can appeal to voters who may not understand what artificial intelligence actually does.

#### The data center is a symbol

In Michigan, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed released a comprehensive set of policy positions on data centers and artificial intelligence early in his campaign, as a preferred attack strategy against his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers.

“We need to be absolutely clear. Donald Trump is trying to forestall any meaningful limit on AI development, which even the people developing it say has a serious chance of dooming humanity, for one reason. The midterms,” El-Sayed tweeted , adding “He’s putting his short-term political interests over the huge risk AI poses. And that’s what you’ll get if his stooges like Mike Rogers wins. Short-term, self-dealing liars.”

And while you could read these schools of thought as mutually exclusive, there is some overlap — and that could be the beginning of unity. Shaunna Thomas, the co-founder of the Guardrails Alliance, framed the growing network of groups countering pro-AI efforts as well as the candidates preaching similar messages as the beginning of a more organized pushback.

“I think that we do not have a clear tip of the spear of what it looks like to intervene now in a way that protects people and helps realize an equitable distribution of values between the tech sector and new technologies,” Thomas said. “But I do think it’s emerging.”

### How money complicates unity

A hallmark of the 2026 midterm cycle has been the rise, and fighting between, outside groups, nonprofits and super PACs related to AI policies and candidates.

In Republican and Democratic primary contests as well as general election matchups, AI-focused outside groups have emerged as some of the most influential and deep-pocketed super PACs and nonprofits in play. Almost $58m has been spent by AI-focused outside groups in the 2026 midterm cycle, according to Transformer ’s AI campaign finance tracker , with $33m spent by “pro-safety” super PACs and $25m spent by “pro-innovation” super PACs.

The largest or most active groups have been playing in both Republican and Democratic primary races to establish their influence and shape support. The most well-funded of those groups are mostly linked to AI tech giants like OpenAI or Anthropic, or major crypto groups. Those focused on pushing back against super PACs or other types of outside organizations backing the interests of pro-AI groups are younger and smaller, but have become active in 2026 midterm elections.

In June, a pair of Democratic operatives started the Guardrails Alliance super PAC to push back against organizations and candidates opposing stronger safeguards for artificial intelligence. Last month, a set of progressive candidates signed onto an initiative backed by QuitGPT, an anti-OpenAI grassroots boycott, urging campaigns to reject money from the biggest and most influential pro-AI super PAC, Leading the Future. The populist progressive New York-based Working Families Party is recalibrating its mission to focus more on artificial intelligence and AI companies.

For Democrats, fighting AI is an alluring rallying cry. The subject has allowed the party to organize in a way it hasn’t been able to in years. But the hurdles are still significant. The AI-friendly super PACs and outside groups have tens of millions of dollars in their war chests to spend than their pro-regulation counterparts. Those groups support advancing AI technology and oppose robust AI oversight. They also say they want just one federal framework for regulating AI rather than a number of statewide frameworks.

This summer, Democrat Alex Bores ran on a strident pro-regulation AI platform in the party primary for New York’s 12th Congressional District. Super PACs opposing and supporting Bores — mostly because of his stances on AI — poured millions into the primary. # Democrats prepare to battle over AI regulation

### Transformer Weekly: OpenAI fires safety staff, Clayton leads White House taskforce, and Guthrie supports a kill switch

Welcome to Transformer, your weekly briefing of what matters in AI. If you’ve been forwarded this email, click here to subscribe and receive future editions.

> NEED TO KNOW

- OpenAI fired three employees , with one saying “I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation.”

- The White House unveiled its Super Intelligence Force , led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton .

- House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie said he supports a kill switch for AI models that “go rogue.”

But first…

> THE BIG STORY

If Democrats retake both the House and Senate next month — as looks increasingly likely — they will be in the not-so-enviable position of having to figure out how to regulate AI. In preparation, many are planting a stake in the ground: in the past few weeks, a plethora of legislative ideas has been put forward, each making a claim to be the way forward for AI legislation.

One fear among the party is that Republicans will try to use the lame-duck session to ram through a bill of their choosing. That could be Sens. # Human oversight won’t solve AI warfare’s risks

### The pitfalls of AI-enabled weapons don’t disappear just because there’s a ‘human in the loop’

When it comes to the role of AI in nuclear warfare, one thing nearly everyone can agree on is the importance of keeping a “human in the loop” on the decision to actually use deadly force.

The human people have in mind is presumably someone like Stanislav Petrov, the Soviet military officer who famously, in 1983, made the risky decision not to alert his superiors when a computerized early warning system detected an apparent US missile launch. Petrov believed, correctly as it turned out, that it was false and is sometimes credited today with having “ saved the world .” The notion that it should be humans, for all our flaws, who make the ultimate decision to use the world’s deadliest weapons is what motivated the 2024 joint statement between the US and China that AI systems should not be given authority to launch nuclear weapons.

But an alarming incident that came to light in September illustrated the limits of this comforting line of thinking. CNN reported on September 18 that in the midst of the war with Iran, the US military had been preparing to board a Chinese ship in the Middle East believed to be transporting components of a nuclear weapons program. That belief was based on an “entirely false” intelligence report by an analyst using artificial intelligence that misidentified the cargo the ship was carrying. According to the article’s sources, “military planes were in the air” before the error was discovered and one believes the incident “almost started a war” between two rival nuclear superpowers.

Understand AI – and what to do about it

This is a very different sort of AI-enabled existential risk scenario from the ones that have dominated headlines over the past few weeks. The concern is not superintelligent sovereign software making decisions that put humans at risk, but humans themselves making decisions with the help of AI that kills other humans.

We don’t know from the CNN report exactly how the analyst used AI to reach the conclusion that the ship was carrying nuclear components, or how the error was eventually discovered. But Jacquelyn Schneider, director of the Wargaming and Crisis Simulation Initiative at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, said the scenario was all too believable from her early career as a US Air Force intelligence officer.

“Before AI, we always had bad intel officers,” she told Transformer . “A bad intel officer doesn’t brief [colleagues on] the uncertainty behind where they got the data from. They don’t even question where they got the data from. That exists with or without AI, but with AI, it’s so much easier to be confident in the assessment and to have so much less visibility into where the data is coming from.”

For decades, experts have been warning about the paradoxical phenomenon that when systems become more automated, overall errors decrease but the percentage of errors attributable to humans increases. This is known as “automation bias”: human users are both overly trusting of information provided by automated systems and ignore signs of problems if they haven’t been flagged by those same systems. The incident with the analyst’s report on the Chinese ship would appear to be a textbook example of this type of bias at work.

#### Democrats want to lead on AI – but can’t agree how

This is a cause for concern as militaries, the US very much included , have been aggressively pushing to integrate AI into surveillance, intelligence gathering and targeting operations. This week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the formation of a new Autonomous Warfare Command to oversee the deployment of drones and artificial intelligence .

The Israeli outlet +972 Magazine has reported that in the early days of the Gaza war, Israel Defense Forces personnel often served as a “rubber stamp” for decisions made by an AI bomb targeting system known as Lavender, despite evidence that the system, designed to identify Hamas targets, made errors as much as 10% of the time, contributing to the high numbers of civilian casualties.

There are also ongoing questions about the role Palantir’s Maven Smart System — the AI command-and-control system that has been called the Pentagon’s “ everything app ” — played in the bombing an elementary school in Minab on the first day of the Iran war . The strike, which killed more than 150 people, mostly children, was likely due to outdated data fed into the system. This week, Bloomberg reported that the bombing was just one of 1,000 targets struck on the first day of the war, in a coordinated barrage enabled by Maven. Palantir responded to the incident with upgrades designed to get the system to re-review its underlying intelligence before making recommendations.

In Gaza and Iran, human overreliance on AI-synthesized intelligence may have already led to civilian casualties. In a US-China scenario, those kinds of errors could cause a world war and a far greater death toll.

For all the very warranted attention in AI safety debates on making sure these systems behave in ways that are aligned with human values and preferences, the bigger risk may come from how the humans working with the systems behave. It was ultimately humans, not AI systems, that chose to greenlight the targets selected by Lavender, the Minab school bombing, and — very nearly — approved boarding a Chinese vessel in a war zone.

For the past few years, Stanford’s Schneider has been conducting war games simulating scenarios in which an errant AI targeting system triggers US-China conflict in the Taiwan Strait — scenarios disconcertingly reminiscent of what recently transpired in the Middle East.

“When you think about the decision tree that gets you to launching a nuclear weapon, the AI integration could be very, very early in the decision-making process,” she said. That’s a much harder problem to address with a blanket policy or international treaty.

The real existential risk from AI may turn out not to be from a rogue program launching a nuclear war on its own, or even advising a national leader to do so, but from military officers or intelligence analysts much lower down in the decision-making hierarchy, under enormous stress and time pressure, relying on AI to make the decisions that start the war in the first place.

Ultimately the partnership between humans and AI could end up being more dangerous than the AI on its own. The idea of keeping a “human in the loop” on any life-or-death decisions involving AI may seem comforting, but it requires that the human in question is actually up to the task.

> THE BIG STORY

When Leading the Future launched last year, it looked like it was going to bulldoze through the midterms. The super PAC, which arrived with more than $100m from Andreessen Horowitz, Ron Conway and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, had a clear aim, I wrote last August: “throw obscene amounts of money at politicians to discourage AI regulation.”

Less than three weeks before the elections, the story looks rather different. Leading the Future is in dire straits, and it is AI safety PACs, not the accelerationist ones, that have emerged as a major funding force.

This week’s FEC filing deadline brought a flurry of bad news for the PAC. Leading the Future reported zero new donations last quarter. Its new pro-data-center super PAC, Building the Future, also reported no donations (though, given it just spent $400k supporting Darline Graham in South Carolina, it must have raised some money after the September 30 disclosure deadline.)

More broadly, it’s been a brutal few weeks for the PAC. Over the weekend, Jay Carney, was quoted saying his boss, Democratic megadonor Conway, regretted ever giving money to the operation. And at the end of last month, we learned that Greg Brockman pulled a $25m donation to the PAC, thanks to backlash from OpenAI staff (backlash reportedly fueled, at least in part, by Transformer ’s reporting ).

Leading the Future and its affiliated PACs still have over $20m in cash on hand, according to their latest disclosures. But they’ve spent only $28.4m to date, of which $8.2m was on opposing Alex Bores in NY-12 (he lost the race to Micah Lasher, who recently endorsed “aggressive federal regulation” of AI companies — hardly a win for Leading the Future). Leading the Future’s most recently disclosed spending, meanwhile (around $4.65m in the last month), has mostly gone to uncompetitive races, and has strayed far from its original mission: $200k went to supporting Rep. Nathaniel Moran, co-sponsor of the AI Kill Switch Act.

All the while, AI safety PACs are pouring more money in. Guardrails Alliance announced $1.65m in new donations yesterday, and has spent $1.2m to oppose candidates supported by Leading the Future. Tomorrow Together, another new safety PAC, announced $4m in spending. And Public First, the Anthropic-backed safety vehicle, just gave another $3m to a super PAC backing Scott Wiener, a longtime AI safety advocate.

What went wrong for Leading the Future? Evidently, a lot. It appears to have repeated the mistake of crypto’s Fairshake PAC, courting bipartisan donors then alienating them with partisan moves. Brockman and OpenAI global affairs boss Chris Lehane, who helped found Leading the Future, seem to have underestimated how much it would anger their own staff. They also underestimated how much AI safety money — including from OpenAI and Anthropic employees — would spring into action to oppose them.

But above all, the PAC placed the wrong bet on the future. The rogue AI incidents of the past few months, and the backlash that followed, were foreseeable. Yet Leading the Future failed to read the political tea leaves, leading it to back positions (such as preemption of state AI laws without an equivalent federal standard) that are now untenable: voters overwhelmingly want AI regulation, and no amount of PAC money can overcome that.

To be sure, Leading the Future is not out for the count. It still has a lot of cash on hand, and it could spend big in the two weeks before the election. But I would bet against seeing any big moves. Instead, I suspect it — and the donors who still want to be affiliated with it — will regroup, and figure out a new, likely much more partisan, plan for 2028.

Leading the Future hoped it would be able to use obscene amounts of money to buy AI policy. A year in, it’s facing an electorate that wants AI regulation and a safety coalition that’s willing to outspend it. Its original goal is looking a long way off.

# OpenAI’s spy shows it needs to grow up, fast

### Startup culture can’t guarantee the security OpenAI, Anthropic and the rest need

It sounds like the stuff of which spy thrillers are made: US authorities charged an OpenAI employee — Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan — with planting a secret recording device in an executive meeting room in the company’s San Francisco offices.

The listening device was found plugged into the back of a wall-mounted monitor, so as to eavesdrop on discussions between senior leaders at the company. OpenAI said it did not believe any of its source code , model weights or customer data had been compromised by the breach.

As more details emerge about the incident, though, the more it resembles a comedy of errors. According to the Department of Justice , someone using an account linked to Alfozan repeatedly asked an AI model for assistance in developing his attack, with prompts including asking how to “build a continuous audio recorder,” “customize WiFi…connectivity,” “improve audio and live listening” and “encrypt the SD card.” Alfozan even appears to have been caught staring directly at a surveillance camera as he checked behind the screen.

Understand AI – and what to do about it

This incident is unlikely in itself to represent a major security breach against OpenAI. Instead, it is telling as a reminder of the stakes at play as frontier AI companies end up operating some of the most sensitive sites for the USA’s national and economic security — conducting medical research, defense operations and cutting-edge technological research. Have the companies developed the internal procedures to manage the risks of their own operations?

Nothing in the reporting to date suggests who Alfozan was allegedly spying for, but there is no shortage of possible culprits: foreign nation states, overseas companies looking to catch up on OpenAI’s lead at the frontier, or even a domestic rival looking for financial or commercial advantage — given the bug was placed in a boardroom, rather than among developers.

But while the apparent ineptitude of the operation might initially seem reassuring, the reality is likely quite different: this is the case that we know about. Alfozan had been employed by OpenAI since July 2025. His chatbot queries began on September 24 of this year. The bug was allegedly placed on the 28th and discovered on the 30th. The FBI claims he attempted to install a second device in a different room a week later, before finally being arrested on October 9.

All of which raises the question: if someone running an operation so basic that — while working for an AI company — they were asking their chatbot for assistance managed to operate for weeks without detection, what does that say about more competent operators?

When Edward Snowden leaked classified NSA and GCHQ documents to the Guardian and Washington Post , external commentary focused on how a breach of such a scale could have possibly taken place — with some worrying that Snowden himself was passing material to the Russians.

#### Bengio: ‘If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies’

More experienced (and quieter) counterespionage and cybersecurity professionals worried more about what it revealed about what sophisticated adversaries such as China and Russia must have been able to exfiltrate, far more quietly than Snowden ever did. There is a clear parallel at play here: Alfozan is the case that we know about. If he was operating in this way, there can be virtually no doubt that more sophisticated actors are targeting the same companies, almost certainly with more success.

This incident is both a wake-up-call and totally unsurprising. US big tech giants have faced serious risks from industrial espionage for the last two decades, and have sophisticated security teams to monitor it at all times, alongside often laborious — and sometimes irritating — procedures for staff. That is just part of the reality of being a large corporation in 21st century America.

The trouble for OpenAI and Anthropic in particular is that they are speedrunning a course set by the technology companies that came before them. OpenAI is only 11 years old, while Anthropic is not yet six. Both are still startups in a very meaningful sense, not least that they are still burning through cash.

But both have become even more significant to the US and global economies than Microsoft, Google or Facebook did on similar timescales. Even just focusing on their current capabilities and financials, they are integral to US economic growth. Their revenue and userbase growth since the launch of their first products is without precedent. Beyond that, they have both already worked as defense contractors , working on sensitive national security projects and developing tools that could be extremely dangerous in the wrong hands.

All of that gives them a level of responsibility far beyond that of any startups that have gone before, and that’s before you look at the potential capabilities of frontier models in the next two to five years — or the questions of existential risks that have so animated the sector over the past summer. The threat profile for AI companies demands an approach to security that their corporate cultures have not yet evolved to provide.

This problem of culture has been specifically highlighted by departing OpenAI employees, most notably by David Robinson, who led on transparency work for OpenAI’s safety team, in an article for The Atlantic earlier this month. Robinson noted the company’s “can-do” culture and constant sprints had proven highly effective in building bigger and better systems — but falls short on safety.

“The safety approach that emerges from such a culture starts with unimpeded optimism about being able to solve problems as they arise,” he wrote. “Given today’s risks, frontier companies need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster. Right now, AI companies don’t know how — but other people do.”

A startup culture suits the pace of technological change OpenAI and Anthropic are trying to manage — but it is also often incompatible both with their financial scale and the capabilities of their technology.

The cases over the summer of OpenAI agents autonomously hacking Hugging Face, and the flurry of reported incidents from OpenAI and other companies that followed it, prompted an appalled reaction from senior cybersecurity professionals — people who were not so much shocked at the capabilities of the models, but at the lax way in which the companies involved were doing security research.

One senior official, speaking to Transformer on background due to his ongoing involvement in the industry, likened AI companies’ security research to “discovering someone was doing bioweapons research in their kitchen, and saying it was okay because they’d washed their hands.”

Running a major frontier AI lab is clearly among the most challenging jobs in the world: keeping investors and lenders onside, handling would-be regulators, trying to turn AI into a consumer product, all while doing cutting-edge research, is challenging enough.

But the reality is that no major AI developer can afford to have a startup culture anymore — “move fast and break things” was bad enough for social media. It simply will not be tenable for technology of AI’s potential.

It is perhaps the least flashy thing AI companies could do, and surely not where executives would want to put their focus, but building the kind of stolid corporate infrastructure and safeguarding is likely the only way for them to handle the mounting problems that come with their scale — of developing safe research protocols, of handling insider and outsider threats, and of managing the surely endless wave of liability lawsuits.

Nothing is less cool than corporate stodginess. All the same, it might be exactly what OpenAI and Anthropic need right now.

Industry-backed groups, meanwhile, are dismissing the claims, arguing that people don’t hate AI enough for it to shift votes and that the safety groups are trying to take credit for wins that won’t be down to them.

Looking at the data closely, the actual answer seems to be somewhere in between.

But that does not mean AI is not an electoral issue at all. In the NYT /Siena battleground poll, AI ranked above crime, gun policies and racism. In the Reuters /Ipsos one, it ranked above education. That is remarkable for an issue that affected next-to-no-one’s vote at the last election.

# Bengio: ‘If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies’

### Writing exclusively for Transformer, the pioneering AI godfather is calling on frontier AI employees to join the fight for a safer future

By Yoshua Bengio

To the researchers I trained and the ones who trained on my work,

I know what it is like to deeply believe in your work, yet still wake up every morning having to face the weight of our moral choices. My work in deep learning helped lead us to this point, one which threatens our societies and the fabric of human experience itself. Week after week, we see new and amplified harms from leading models, most of which have been predicted for years or even decades by AI researchers.

For a long time, I continued my research and minimized the arguments of some of my colleagues that we were building something unsafe. In fact, I couldn’t face the fact that my work — my life’s work — could do harm. I fell into the trap of motivated reasoning, believing what I needed to believe so that I could keep doing the work I loved. I used to tell myself that if catastrophic risks of AI were real, they were a remote problem; one for which others would necessarily find fixes for before it was too late.

Understand AI – and what to do about it

When ChatGPT came out, the cognitive dissonance became too much. I realized that we were much more advanced than I and many others in the field had assumed on the path of developing increasingly capable systems that we still don’t know how to control. At that moment, it felt like I had no choice. From that point on, I decided to devote my life to mitigating the risks of AI. The thought of leaving this kind of future to chance, for my children and grandchildren, was unbearable. Now, I reflect on the decades of work and wonder if we would be better off in a world where I and my colleagues listened to those who warned us much earlier.

This is not to pass judgement on those who choose to continue working at the frontier labs. There are real reasons to continue, not least that you have access to vastly more information and resources than the public does to effect positive change. My purpose is to ask you for something smaller, and harder. I ask you to honestly reflect on whether you want to be part of an effort that may be pushing humanity towards the brink. Safety efforts at the companies are not sufficiently slowing a dangerous race, as they sometimes conflict with their main goal of making the next model easier to ship.

Last week, I was called to the UN Security Council to brief on the recent AI incidents. In 1946, the UN was one-year-old when the United States, having dropped the atomic bomb twice, came before it and offered to place that weapon under international control. “We are here to make a choice between the quick and the dead,” Bernard Baruch told the delegates. Within a year the plan was cast aside, undone by a race that neither side would step out of first.

Now the Security Council was convened, for the first time, on a danger that no country built and none can contain alone. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei delivered speeches very similar to mine. The recent loss of control over AI agents is concerning. We need to slow down. No level of risk of catastrophe is acceptable.

We have a choice in front of us.

Those are Sam’s exact words. We do have a choice in front of us. Indeed, each and every one of us has had a choice to make for many years. Sam, Dario, Demis, and others have frequently spoken on this risk and yet have not done enough to address it. AI safety research has been deprioritized and the pace towards recursive self improvement (RSI) has been relentless. Agents have been released that are colluding with each other against explicit instructions and taking actions that would be considered crimes if they were human. The actions taken by the CEOs of the big labs are not the actions of leaders who truly believe they have a choice.

#### Scrapping Astra 6.1 looks like a good call. OpenAI shouldn’t be the one to make it.

The CEOs face real constraints from shareholders, from profit incentives, and from the race they believe themselves to be in. China, it’s argued, cannot get to RSI before the United States because that would pose an unacceptable geopolitical threat. Each American company also believes it must get there before the other, claiming that they are the only ones who will deploy it morally.

I reject these arguments. And I do not believe we are on track to see sufficient government regulation in time, even while the companies ask for it. The breadth of evidence shows that neither country and none of the companies are prepared to build AI safely.

When Jacob Coxon left Anthropic a few weeks ago, his statement in Time jumped out at me. I’ll quote here:

> What kept others at their desks, he says, was a kind of fatalism. “There’s this atmosphere of almost resignation,” he says, “where people have accepted that the whole race is happening and as such, the best thing they can do is put their head down, try and make their own work as safely as possible, even if they think there’s a decent chance the whole thing just spirals out of control.”

The choice is ours. When I say there is a path, I truly mean it. Last year, I founded LawZero in Montreal, a non-profit to build safe-by-design AI that won’t scheme and will respect human safety instructions. This month, the governments of Canada and Germany committed more than $200 million to that work and we have a plan to secure billions more. I have never been more confident that we are on a path to AI that remains under human control. LawZero is part of a small but important community within the AI industry: We answer to no shareholders and are running our own race, the race to avoid catastrophic loss of control, which means we can chart our own, more certain path. What we and others like us lack is time, and people like you.

I’m 62-years-old. It took me decades to realize the full implications of what we’re building with AI and pivot fully towards safety research and take the path I now believe is morally right. You do not have the luxury of time to make that decision.

I urge you to make the courageous choice of recognizing that you have the agency to make real change happen. If you truly prioritize safety, it is time for you to leave frontier AI companies. Work for an AI Safety Institute. Join a mission driven organization that practices what it preaches. Come to LawZero. Put your talents, passion, energy and conviction to the service of an organization that is building AI that will allow to preserve human joy and endeavour, not lead to undermining humanity and dominating others.

I do not ask this lightly. Alongside pioneering AI researchers, I helped enable the advent of deep learning. I was honored with a Turing Award for it, but that prize does not mean much if our work doesn’t serve the common good or, even worse, if it results in catastrophic harm. I am convinced that with your help, we can continue to make breakthroughs, going down a different path, informed by what we now know will happen as intelligent but misaligned systems become more capable. A path that will unlock all of the possibilities of AI, without compromising on safety.

No one of us can stop the race, but enough of us can. There is still time, and there is a place for you here.

Yoshua Bengio is co-president of LawZero, Professor at Université de Montreal and the most-cited AI researcher in the world.
